Matrix Multiplication Refresher

Before we jump back into quantum mechanics, I want to review a quick linear algebra concept based on the recent quiz. As a class, we did pretty well, but I noticed a common misconception regarding matrix-vector multiplication.

Let’s say we have a 3 \times 3 matrix multiplied by a 3-dimensional column vector: \begin{equation} \begin{pmatrix} a & b & c \\ d & e & f \\ g & h & i \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} v_1 \\ v_2 \\ v_3 \end{pmatrix} \tag{1} \end{equation}

If you are new to linear algebra, it is tempting to multiply column-wise. I saw a few folks calculating the first term as a v_1 + d v_2 + g v_3. This is incorrect!

The correct way to perform this operation is row-wise. Imagine physically ripping the column vector out of the page, rotating it horizontally, and dropping it onto the first row of the matrix. You multiply the matching elements and add them up. Then, you bring that horizontal vector down to the second row, and so on.

Here is the proper mathematical execution: \begin{equation} \tag{2} \begin{pmatrix} a & b & c \\ d & e & f \\ g & h & i \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} v_1 \\ v_2 \\ v_3 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} a v_1 + b v_2 + c v_3 \\ d v_1 + e v_2 + f v_3 \\ g v_1 + h v_2 + i v_3 \end{pmatrix} \end{equation}

Keep this row-wise operation in mind. We are going to be seeing it quite a bit as we build our quantum mechanical models.

The Schrödinger Equation: Two Paths

Last week, we introduced the Schrödinger equation. This equation is the jack-of-all-trades in quantum mechanics. In principle, if you can solve it, you can know pretty much everything there is to know about a molecule or a material system.

Specifically, we are looking for two things when we solve this equation:

  1. Allowed energy levels: The specific energies that electrons can possess in a molecule.

  2. Quantum states (Wavefunctions): The shape of the electron cloud surrounding the molecule, which tells us where the electrons are most likely to be found.

Let’s look at the general form of the Schrödinger equation: \begin{equation} \tag{3} \hat{H}|\psi\rangle = E|\psi\rangle \end{equation}

Here, \hat{H} is the Hamiltonian, which is the energy operator. When I hear "operator," I think of Tank from the movie The Matrix at his computer console. If Tank were an energy operator, he’d be a Hamiltonian! Mathematically, an operator is just an object that "does stuff" to a state.

The symbol |\psi\rangle is the Greek letter psi inside a funky bracket called a ket. This represents our quantum state (or wavefunction). When the Hamiltonian operates on this state, it magically spits out E, the allowed energy level, multiplied by that exact same quantum state |\psi\rangle.

There are two main ways to represent and solve this equation: using differential equations or using linear algebra.

In a previous introductory class, you likely saw the differential equation version. In that framework, the Hamiltonian operator involves calculus—specifically, a second derivative with respect to position, plus a potential energy term. The quantum state is a continuous function, and the energy is a constant.

In this class, we are going to use the linear algebra version. The Hamiltonian becomes a matrix, the quantum state becomes a vector (an eigenvector), and the energy becomes an eigenvalue.

Why Differential Equations Get Messy

To understand why we prefer the linear algebra approach for materials, let’s look at what happens when we try to use differential equations on a very simple molecule.

Instead of a single atom, let’s bond two atoms together. To keep it as simple as possible, we will look at the hydrogen molecular ion, \text{H}_2^+. This system has two protons and only one electron. How hard could that be?

Let’s attempt to sketch out the Hamiltonian operator for this system in differential form. The Hamiltonian consists of kinetic energy and potential energy.

The kinetic energy term for the electron looks like this: \begin{equation} \text{Kinetic Energy} = -\frac{\hbar^2}{2m} \nabla^2 \tag{4} \end{equation} The inverted triangle (\nabla^2) is the 3D version of a second derivative.

The real devil is in the potential energy term. We have to account for electrostatic interactions based on charges. Positive charges repel each other, and opposite charges attract. For our \text{H}_2^+ ion, we have three distinct interactions to track:

  1. The repulsion between the two positive protons (separated by distance R).

  2. The attraction between proton A and the electron (separated by distance r_a).

  3. The attraction between proton B and the electron (separated by distance r_b).

Putting it all together, the Hamiltonian operator looks like this: \begin{equation} \tag{5} \hat{H} = \underbrace{-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m} \nabla^2}_{\text{Kinetic}} + \underbrace{\frac{e^2}{4\pi\epsilon_0 R}}_{\text{p-p repulsion}} - \underbrace{\frac{e^2}{4\pi\epsilon_0 r_a}}_{\text{p-e attraction}} - \underbrace{\frac{e^2}{4\pi\epsilon_0 r_b}}_{\text{p-e attraction}} \end{equation}

This is already looking awful, and this is for the simplest molecule in existence! What if we look at a neutral hydrogen molecule (\text{H}_2) with two electrons? We would have to add three more interaction terms (electron-electron repulsion, and two more proton-electron attractions). What if we look at a benzene ring with six carbons and a bunch of hydrogens? The number of interaction terms explodes.

Trying to capture every single interaction in a differential equation is a tremendously hard problem. To get around this, we are going to use a linear algebra shortcut.

If we upgraded from the H_2^+ ion to a neutral H_2 molecule, how many total interaction terms would we have to track in the potential energy part of our differential equation?

We would have to track six total interactions! We keep the original three (proton-proton repulsion and two proton-electron attractions), but we have to add three more: the repulsion between the two electrons, and two new attractions between the second electron and each proton. This explosion of terms is exactly why we need our linear algebra shortcut.

The Linear Algebra Rescue: LCAO

Since we do not know the exact shape of a molecular orbital, and the differential equation is too hard to solve directly, we are going to make an educated guess.

We will assume that the molecular wavefunction is built out of simpler building blocks that we already know: atomic orbitals. Specifically, we will use the 1s atomic orbitals of the individual hydrogen atoms.

We construct the molecular orbital by adding these atomic orbitals together, each multiplied by a weighting coefficient. This technique is called a Linear Combination of Atomic Orbitals (LCAO).

Mathematically, our molecular wavefunction |\psi_{\text{mol}}\rangle is: \begin{equation} \tag{6} |\psi_{\text{mol}}\rangle = c_1 |\psi_1\rangle + c_2 |\psi_2\rangle \end{equation} Where:

  • |\psi_1\rangle is the 1s atomic orbital of the first hydrogen atom.

  • |\psi_2\rangle is the 1s atomic orbital of the second hydrogen atom.

  • c_1 and c_2 are the coefficients that dictate how much of each atomic orbital contributes to the final molecule.

Because we are using two building blocks, our Schrödinger equation becomes a tidy 2 \times 2 matrix eigenvalue problem: \begin{equation} \tag{7} \begin{pmatrix} H_{11} & H_{12} \\ H_{21} & H_{22} \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} c_1 \\ c_2 \end{pmatrix} = E \begin{pmatrix} c_1 \\ c_2 \end{pmatrix} \end{equation}

Let’s break down what the elements of this Hamiltonian matrix represent:

  • Diagonal elements (H_{11}, H_{22}): These are the on-site energies. This is the energy of an electron buzzing around a standalone hydrogen atom. We will call this value -\alpha. It is a negative number because the atom is energetically stable. From spectroscopy, we know this value is exactly -13.6 \text{ eV}.

  • Off-diagonal elements (H_{12}, H_{21}): These represent the interaction or coupling energy between the adjacent atoms. This is what allows bonding to happen. We will call this value -\beta. It is also negative to represent a stable interaction. For hydrogen, this is approximately -2.25 \text{ eV}.

Substituting these symbols into our matrix equation, we get: \begin{equation} \tag{8} \begin{pmatrix} -\alpha & -\beta \\ -\beta & -\alpha \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} c_1 \\ c_2 \end{pmatrix} = E \begin{pmatrix} c_1 \\ c_2 \end{pmatrix} \end{equation}

Why do we define both the on-site energy (-\alpha) and the coupling energy (-\beta) as negative numbers in our Hamiltonian matrix?

In physics, negative energy represents a stable, bound state. An electron buzzing around a single proton is energetically stable compared to floating freely in space, so its on-site energy is negative. Similarly, the coupling energy is negative because the interaction between the adjacent atoms creates a stable bond that lowers the overall energy of the system.

Solving for the Energy Levels of H_2

Now we have a legitimate equation that we can solve using standard linear algebra. Our first goal is to find the allowed energy levels, which are the eigenvalues (E).

To find the eigenvalues, we subtract E from the diagonal elements and set the determinant of the resulting matrix to zero: \begin{equation} \tag{9} \begin{vmatrix} -\alpha - E & -\beta \\ -\beta & -\alpha - E \end{vmatrix} = 0 \end{equation}

To calculate the determinant, we cross-multiply the diagonal terms and subtract the product of the off-diagonal terms: \begin{align} (-\alpha - E)(-\alpha - E) - (-\beta)(-\beta) &= 0 \tag{10}\\ (-\alpha - E)^2 - \beta^2 &= 0 \tag{11}\\ (-\alpha - E)^2 &= \beta^2 \tag{12} \end{align}

Taking the square root of both sides (and remembering that a square root yields both a positive and a negative root), we get: \begin{equation} -\alpha - E = \pm \beta \tag{13} \end{equation}

Solving for E, we find our two allowed energy levels: \begin{equation} \tag{14} E = -\alpha \pm \beta \end{equation}

This simple 2 \times 2 matrix gives us a profound physical result. When two hydrogen atoms come together, their original isolated energy levels (-\alpha) split into two new molecular energy levels:

  • Lower Energy (Bonding): E_{\text{low}} = -\alpha - \beta. Because \beta is a positive magnitude (we defined the interaction as -\beta), subtracting it lowers the energy further. Electrons are lazy and want to live in the lowest energy state possible. By dropping into this state, the system saves energy, which is why the atoms bond in the first place!

  • Higher Energy (Anti-bonding): E_{\text{high}} = -\alpha + \beta. This is the evil twin of the bonding orbital. It sits at a higher energy than the isolated atoms.

Visualizing the Molecular Orbitals

What do these states actually look like? If we look at an isolated 1s atomic orbital, it looks like a pointy function—an exponential decay centered on the proton, showing that the electron is most likely to be found near the nucleus.

When we form the bonding orbital (corresponding to E_{\text{low}}), the two atomic orbitals are added together with the same sign (c_1 = 1, c_2 = 1). The functions overlap and elevate in the middle, meaning there is a high probability of finding the electron between the two protons. This shared electron cloud holds the molecule together.

When we form the anti-bonding orbital (corresponding to E_{\text{high}}), the atomic orbitals are combined with opposite signs (c_1 = 1, c_2 = -1). One of the pointy hats flips upside down. Right in the middle between the two atoms, the functions cancel out, creating a "node" where there is zero probability of finding an electron. Without electron density between the protons to shield them, they repel each other, pushing the atoms apart.

Mathematically, what creates the "node" (zero electron probability) in the middle of the anti-bonding orbital?

The node appears because the two 1s atomic orbitals are combined with opposite signs (c_1 = 1 and c_2 = -1). When you add a positive function to an inverted (negative) function of the exact same shape, they cancel out to zero right in the middle. Without that shared electron cloud to hold things together, the bare protons repel!

By using a simple 2 \times 2 matrix, we bypassed the nightmare of differential equations and successfully derived the energy levels and orbital shapes that explain why hydrogen atoms bond. Next time, we will apply this technique to even more complicated molecules!
